abstract: Rapid urbanisation and largely unplanned development in Indian cities have been drawing increasing ethnographic attention in recent years. Even though other-than-human beings are an integral part of these spaces, the city is still most often understood from a human perspective. Simultaneously, nonhumans actively shape and reshape their environments through everyday behavioural choices - choices that are not only ecological, but also socioeconomic, and often influenced by their interactions and relationships with human beings. In this paper, we adopt a mixed-methods, etho-ethnographic approach to explore a curious case of other-than-human alloparenting within largely affective dog - lifeworlds in the Indian megapolis of Delhi. We focus on a triadic relationship between two co-territorial female street dogs -- Bhuri and Kali -- and a particular human caregiver -- Kishan -- that reveal how these two dogs, sharing the same territory within Gur Mandi, an informal settlement in north Delhi, adjust their allo/parenting behaviour in response to their independent social interactions with the human residents of the area. This more-than-human narrative suggests that street dogs are not merely passive inhabitants of the city, but sentient, affective participants, who shape urban life through their everyday interactions. Moreover, the counter-intuitive shifts that we observed in multibeing parenting behaviour reflect how human presence could configure short-term social interactions and the long-term relationships between nonhuman beings in their shared spaces.
